phil:raoul-vaneigem: Raoul Vaneigem (born 1934) is a Belgian Situationist theorist whose The Revolution of Everyday Life (1967) argues that commodity society reduces lived experience to mere survival, mediated by images and roles. Against this he sets 'lived poetry': creativity, play, and direct participation reclaimed from the spectacle. His insistence that everyday alienation is political makes him a natural touchstone for critiques of consumer culture and fan practice.
phil:ivan-illich: Ivan Illich (1926–2002) was an Austrian-born critic of institutional life whose Deschooling Society and Tools for Conviviality argue that modern institutions progressively monopolize the very needs they claim to serve - schooling produces dependency on teachers, medicine on doctors. He counterposed 'convivial' tools, which people control and use for their own ends, to industrial tools that shape people to their demands. His work is a touchstone for anarchist, environmentalist, and technology criticism.
phil:ortega-y-gasset: José Ortega y Gasset (1883–1955) was a Spanish philosopher best known for The Revolt of the Masses, which analyzes mass man as someone satisfied with what he has, ungrateful for the civilization that produced it, and disinclined to self-examination. His 'ratiovitalism' holds that we live by and through ideas, and his perspectivism denies any view from nowhere - each life is a point of view on the world. He influentially warned that democracy without cultivated minorities can degenerate into mediocrity ruling by numbers.
phil:michael-ruse: Michael Ruse (1940–2024) was a philosopher of biology who spent his career on evolutionary theory, its biological bases of morality, and the evolution-creation controversy. On ethics he defended an evolutionary debunking line: our sense that moral claims are objectively true is an illusion 'fobbed off on us' by our genes to make cooperation work. His work anchors debates about whether morality can survive being given a Darwinian explanation.
phil:ronald-dworkin: Ronald Dworkin (1931–2013) was an American legal and political philosopher who argued that rights are 'trumps' over collective welfare and that law is not separate from morality but a matter of interpretive integrity - reading legal practice as the best it can be. In Life's Dominion he sought a middle way in the abortion and euthanasia debates by relocating the dispute from competing rights to the intrinsic value of life. His account of equality as the sovereign virtue of political community shapes contemporary liberalism.
phil:robert-kane: Robert Kane (born 1938) is the leading defender of libertarian free will, arguing that genuinely free 'self-forming actions' occur in moments of moral conflict where each option is willed and the outcome is settled by the agent's effort rather than prior causes. He locates these moments in indeterminacies in the brain and insists that such freedom is required for ultimate responsibility. His work is the standard sophisticated answer to hard determinism.
phil:stephen-mulhall: Stephen Mulhall (born 1961) is an Oxford philosopher whose On Film (2001) helped found the 'film as philosophy' movement by reading mainstream films - Alien, Blade Runner, the Darkness series - as works that do philosophy rather than merely illustrate it. His work draws on Heidegger, Wittgenstein, and Cavell, and treats popular genres as genuine sites of thinking. The claim that films can philosophize, and his critics' replies, frame current debates about cinematic philosophy.
phil:thomas-wartenberg: Thomas E. Wartenberg is a philosopher of film whose Thinking on Screen defends 'screen philosophy': certain films - The Modern Times of Chaplin, The Matrix, Eternal Sunshine - present and advance philosophical arguments audiovisually, through fictional thought experiments. He answers skeptics who think film can at best illustrate ideas by showing how films create, not just convey, philosophical puzzles. His debate with critics over what counts as 'doing' philosophy structures the field.
phil:bruce-russell: Bruce Russell is an epistemologist and philosopher of film who argues for strict limits on cinema as philosophy: films may dramatize or motivate philosophical puzzles, but the argumentative precision philosophy requires is achievable only in prose. His exchange with defenders of film philosophy turns on whether a film's 'argument' can survive without explicit premises. He represents the strongest skeptical position in the film-as-philosophy debate.
phil:leo-strauss: Leo Strauss (1899–1973) was a political philosopher who read the tradition - especially Machiavelli, Hobbes, and Spinoza - as a single 'quarrel between the ancients and the moderns'. He argued that careful writers hid dangerous truths between the lines (the 'art of esoteric writing'), and that modernity is founded on a lowering of moral horizons from natural right to rights of nature and then history. His mode of reading and his return to classical political rationalism remain deeply influential and contested.
phil:vaclav-havel: Václav Havel (1936–2011) was a Czech playwright, dissident, and later president whose The Power of the Powerless analyzed post-totalitarian society through the greengrocer who displays 'Workers of the world, unite!' - an ideology sustained by everyone's ritual participation. He opposed 'living in truth' to the system's pervasive lie, arguing that dissidence is simply refusing to play along. His thought joins existential authenticity to democratic politics.
phil:georg-lukacs: Georg Lukács (1885–1971) was a Hungarian Marxist philosopher whose History and Class Consciousness developed the theory of reification: under capitalism, social relations between people take on the character of relations between things, and consciousness itself is reshaped accordingly. His earlier Theory of the Novel read the novel form as the epic of a transcendentally homeless world. He remains the central figure for Marxist aesthetics and the critique of bourgeois culture.
phil:francis-hutcheson: Francis Hutcheson (1694–1746) was an Irish-Scottish moral sense theorist who held that we perceive virtue and vice with a special inner sense responding to benevolence, not by reason or self-interest alone. His formulation that action is good in proportion to the happiness it produces anticipates utilitarianism, and his insistence on natural human sociability shaped Hume and Adam Smith. He stands for the Enlightenment claim that morality is rooted in feeling as well as reason.
conviviality: Conviviality is Ivan Illich's ideal of a society in which people control their tools rather than being controlled by them: convivial tools - from telephones to libraries to bicycles - can be used by anyone for ends they choose, while industrial 'manipulative' tools create specialized monopolies and dependence. Illich used the word deliberately, evoking both festivity and sharing tools at a common table. The concept grounds his critique of schooling, medicine, and transport, and has been revived for thinking about social media and digital platforms.
echo-chamber: The echo chamber (Sunstein's 'Daily Me') is the pattern in which people customize their information environment to voices that already agree with them, so that each group hears its own views repeated and amplified back. Sunstein argued that such self-sorting produces fragmentation, group polarization, and the loss of shared experiences democracy needs. The concept organizes debates about social media, algorithmic feeds, and whether online life undermines democratic deliberation.
contextual-privacy: Contextual privacy, articulated as 'contextual integrity' by Helen Nissenbaum, holds that informational privacy is governed by norms tied to specific social contexts - what may be shared in a medical context differs from what may be shared in a friendship or a market. Privacy violations occur when information flows breach the norms of the context in which it was given, even if no sensitive secret is revealed. The framework is now central to data-ethics debates because it explains why 'just collecting public data' can still wrong people.
convergence-culture: Convergence culture is Henry Jenkins's account of a media world in which old and new media collide: content flows across platforms, corporate media and participatory fan practices interpenetrate, and collective intelligence - communities pooling knowledge - becomes a new form of media literacy. Jenkins emphasized that convergence is both technological and social, driven as much by migrating audiences as by industry strategy. The concept frames debates about whether transmedia fandom democratizes culture or supplies free labor to it.
media-ecology-tetrad: Marshall McLuhan's tetrad, from Laws of Media, asks four questions of any technology: what does it enhance, what does it obsolesce, what does it retrieve from obsolescence, and what does it reverse into when pushed to its limits? The point is that media form environments - altering sense ratios and social arrangements regardless of their 'content'. The framework treats every medium as an intervention in the ecology of human attention and practice.
politeness-theory: Politeness theory, developed by Penelope Brown and Stephen Levinson, analyzes how speakers manage 'face': the positive face of wanting to be approved of and the negative face of wanting to be unimpeded. Politeness strategies - directness, hedging, deference, irony - are systematic ways of softening face-threatening acts. The theory turns courtesy into a window on social relationships, power, and distance.
punctum-studium: In Camera Lucida, Roland Barthes distinguishes studium - the coded, general interest a photograph holds as culture - from punctum: the accidental detail that pierces the viewer personally, 'wounding' them beyond any code. The distinction is part of his larger claim that photographs are paradoxical messages without a code, proofs of what has been. Punctum and studium have become standard tools for thinking about images, memory, and mourning.
online-disinhibition-effect: The online disinhibition effect, named by John Suler, is the well-documented loosening of self-restraint when people interact online: anonymity, invisibility, asynchronicity, and the absence of authority cues make people bolder, harsher, or more confiding than they would be face to face. Suler distinguished 'toxic' disinhibition (flaming, cruelty) from 'benign' disinhibition (unusual intimacy and self-disclosure). It is the standard frame for analyzing behavior in pseudonymous and anonymous spaces.
presentation-of-self: Erving Goffman's dramaturgical analysis, from The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life, treats social interaction as performance: individuals manage impressions through a 'front stage' of settings, manner, and appearance, while reserving a 'back stage' where the performance is prepared. Identity, on this view, is not expressed but enacted, and its success depends on the audience's cooperation. The concept is foundational for analyzing self-presentation, now including profiles and avatars.
cicero-friendship: In De Amicitia, Cicero defines friendship as complete agreement in all things divine and human, joined with goodwill and affection - and insists that it can exist only between the good. Unlike Aristotle, he stresses that friendship is not primarily useful: friendships founded on advantage or pleasure collapse when those go, while virtue-based friendship is 'the greatest of all the gifts the gods gave us'. The essay's images - the friend is another self, friendship makes the world wider - anchor the Western tradition on friendship.
excess-of-seeing: The 'excess of seeing' is Mikhail Bakhtin's account of why the other is indispensable to self-knowledge: each of us occupies only one position in the world, so I can never see my own face, back, or the whole of my life - the other always sees in me something I cannot see myself. This surplus, or excess, of the other's vision is what makes ethical and aesthetic relations possible, since I need an 'outside' to be completed. The idea grounds his dialogism: the self is co-authored from a position it cannot occupy.
hume-natural-sympathy: For Hume, sympathy is the psychological mechanism by which the sentiments of others are communicated to us: witnessing another's joy or suffering, we receive a 'contagion' of their feeling via resemblance and imagination, and from it Hume builds both our moral approvals and our sense of justice. Sympathy is natural and involuntary, varying with closeness, yet corrected by general points of view. It makes morality a matter of shared feeling rather than pure reason or self-interest.
ideal-speech-situation: The ideal speech situation is Jürgen Habermas's reconstruction of the conditions under which communication is undistorted: all participants have equal chance to initiate and question, no force except the forceless force of the better argument, and genuine orientation toward consensus. The situation is 'counterfactual' - presupposed by every serious attempt to persuade, though never fully realized. It grounds his discourse ethics and his critique of systematically distorted public spheres.
playbour: Playbour - a fusion of play and labour - names work that presents itself as fun: modders, fan translators, content creators, and social-media users whose enjoyment produces value appropriated by platforms and studios. The concept, associated with Julian Kücklich's study of game modding, highlights the blurring of work and leisure in digital economies and the question of whether playful production is exploitation, self-expression, or both.
power-as-acting-together: For Hannah Arendt, power is never a property of an individual: it 'corresponds to the human ability to act in concert', and it appears and disappears with the group that sustains it. She carefully separates power from strength, force, authority, and violence - violence, being instrumental and dependent on implements, can destroy power but never create it. The account is central to her defense of politics as public, plural action.
interpassivity: Interpassivity, a concept developed by Robert Pfaller and taken up by Slavoj Žižek, names the delegation of one's enjoyment or belief to an object: the canned laughter on the soundtrack laughs for us, the VCR 'watches' films we never see, the mourned portrait weeps for the mourner. Its twin is interactivity - and the point is that supposedly interactive media often interpassively consume for us. The concept unsettles the assumption that engagement and activity belong to the user.
descriptive-vs-prescriptive-normality: To call something 'normal' can mean it is statistically typical, or that it is as it ought to be - and much social power lies in sliding between the two senses. What is descriptive (most people do X) is treated as prescriptive (one should do X), and deviation from the average is re-described as pathology. Distinguishing the senses is a standard move in the philosophy of medicine, disability, and sexuality.
knowledge-is-power: 'Knowledge is power' captures Francis Bacon's doctrine that the goal of learning is not contemplation but effecting things: knowledge of nature's forms gives mastery over nature for the relief of man's estate. Bacon organized science as a collective, state-supported project and tied method - experiment and induction - to utility. The slogan is also the point of departure for critiques (Nietzsche's, Foucault's) of the will-to-know as a will-to-dominate.
metafiction: Metafiction is fiction that draws attention to its own status as constructed artifact - novels with authors inside them, films that acknowledge they are films - thereby blurring the line between world and representation. Postmodern writers used it to explore how texts create the realities they describe, and whether there is any 'outside' to narrative. It raises genuine philosophical questions about self-reference, fiction's truth, and the relation of representation to reality.
evolutionary-ethics: Evolutionary ethics tries to explain morality - and sometimes to ground it - in the theory of evolution: altruism, guilt, and moral norms as adaptations for cooperation among kin and strangers. The descriptive project (explaining why we make moral judgments) must be separated from the justificatory one (whether moral claims are true), and thinkers like Michael Ruse argue that evolution explains our moral sense while undermining its objectivity. The debate tests whether ethics can survive naturalization.
religious-non-realism: Religious non-realism, associated with Don Cupitt, treats God and religious language as human constructs - expressions of spiritual attitude rather than claims about an objectively existing divine reality. On this view religious commitments are true in the way poems and practices are true: they shape lives, not worlds. The position reworks the realism/anti-realism debate for theology and asks what is left of faith without God 'out there'.
purity-of-heart: Purity of Heart Is to Will One Thing is Søren Kierkegaard's meditation on double-mindedness: the heart is pure when it wills the Good for its own sake, undivided by the desire for reward or the fear of punishment. Its searching tests - honestly confronting one's wishes in silence before God - make it a study in sincerity and self-deception. The title phrase has become shorthand for single-minded moral commitment.
iron-cage-rationalization: Max Weber used 'rationalization' for the historical process by which magic and tradition give way to calculation, rules, and efficiency - culminating in bureaucracy, the 'iron cage' in which modern individuals live. Rationalization brings unprecedented technical power at the price of disenchantment: meaning is drained from the world, and persons become cogs in machines of their own making. The concepts frame every critique of organizational, corporate, and technological life.
fabula-syuzhet: The Russian Formalists' distinction between fabula and syuzhet separates the raw events of a story in their chronological, causal order (fabula) from the order and manner in which the work actually presents them (syuzhet). Mysteries, flashbacks, and in medias res openings are syuzhet devices over a fabula the viewer reassembles. The pair is the ancestor of narrative theory's story/discourse distinction and a standard tool for analyzing film structure.
plato-phaedrus-writing: In the Phaedrus, Plato has Socrates recount the myth of Theuth, the god who invented writing and offered it as a drug for memory and wisdom; King Thamus replies that it is a drug for reminding, producing the appearance of wisdom without the reality. Writing cannot choose its readers or answer questions - it says the same thing forever and falls into the wrong hands - and Socrates prefers the living, dialectical word 'written in the soul'. The passage is the founding text of media philosophy and the debate about what technologies of communication do to thought.
intellectual-virtues: Virtue epistemology holds that the excellences of the knower - open-mindedness, intellectual courage, humility, perseverance, fair-mindedness - are central to knowledge, not just logical rules. Intellectual virtues are traits of character that make one a good thinker, and their vices (arrogance, cowardice, dogmatism) explain many failures of belief. The framework has become central to epistemology and to education theory.
lacan-gaze: In Seminar XI, Lacan defines the gaze as the object (objet a) of the scopic drive: the point from which the subject is looked at, preceding and structuring vision - we do not simply look, we are caught in a picture and looked at from outside. The gaze differs from the eye and cannot be controlled by the viewer, which is why images fascinate and unsettle. Lacan's account, via Sartre and Merleau-Ponty, is the backbone of psychoanalytic film theory.
hegel-substance-subject: The phrase 'substance is as much subject as substance' condenses Hegel's Phenomenology: what is real is not a fixed substrate but a self-developing process whose contradictions drive it to know itself - spirit (Geist) is its own product. Absolute knowing is the recognition that the knower and what is known are moments of one self-mediating whole. The claim anchors Hegel's idealism and his critique of Spinoza's static substance.
praxis-vs-poiesis: Aristotle distinguishes poiesis - production, where the point is a product external to the activity (a house) - from praxis, action whose end is internal to the doing itself (just acting, noble acting). Production admits a master-craft (techne); action requires phronesis, practical wisdom about the good life in particulars. The distinction grounds his ethics and resurges in Marx and Arendt as a critique of treating politics or persons as manufacture.
strong-vs-weak-nihilism: Drawing on Nietzsche's contrast between passive and active nihilism, weak nihilism is the exhausted condition in which inherited values lose their authority and nothing is put in their place - decline, resignation, hedonism. Strong nihilism goes through the loss of all values so thoroughly that it becomes a will to destroy values as such, clearing ground for new creation. The distinction lets one ask whether a person, movement, or era is merely collapsing or violently clearing the decks.
three-metamorphoses: In the opening of Thus Spoke Zarathustra, Nietzsche describes three metamorphoses of the spirit: the camel that kneels to bear the weight of 'thou shalt'; the lion that fights the dragon named 'Thou Shalt' and says 'I will'; and finally the child, 'innocence and forgetting', whose sacred Yes begins a new game and a new beginning. The parable compresses his history of morality - obedience, revolt, and the self-legislation of the overhuman. It is among the most quoted passages in philosophy-as-literature.
politics-of-disaffection: The politics of disaffection covers the attitudes - cynicism, alienation, apathy, distrust of institutions - by which citizens distance themselves from mainstream political life, together with the movements that convert disaffection into energy. The analytical question is double-edged: disaffection can corrode democratic participation, or it can be a rational response to captured institutions and the beginning of their reform. The concept bridges political psychology and the critique of technocracy.
bricolage: Bricolage is Claude Lévi-Strauss's picture of mythical thought as working like a handyman (bricoleur): assembling meaning from whatever is at hand, reusing leftover materials with new functions, rather than designing from first principles like an engineer. Derrida extended the term to all discourse - there is no language outside the inherited toolkit - and cultural theory uses it for remix, sampling, and subcultural style. It names creativity as recombination rather than creation ex nihilo.
affect: Affect theory, running from Spinoza through Deleuze to Brian Massumi, treats affect as pre-personal intensity: the capacity to affect and be affected, registered in the body before it is named as emotion. Emotions are captured, named, and socially coded; affects are the passing intensities beneath them. The framework reshaped cultural studies by directing attention to atmosphere, mood, and the bodily resonance of images and music.
labeling-theory: Labeling theory, associated with Howard Becker's Outsiders, holds that deviance is not a property of an act but the consequence of a label applied by others: social groups create deviance by making rules whose violation constitutes deviance, and 'moral entrepreneurs' crusade to have their definitions enforced. Once labeled, a person's self-image and options shift, often producing further deviance - the label becomes a master status. The theory redirects analysis from the deviant act to the audiences and institutions that define it.
matilda-effect: The Matilda Effect, named by Margaret Rossiter after suffragist Matilda Joslyn Gage, is the systematic denial or minimization of women scientists' contributions - their discoveries attributed to male colleagues, their work forgotten or credited to their husbands. It is the gendered counterpart of Robert Merton's Matthew effect, by which the famous accrue ever more credit. The concept is central to feminist philosophy of science and the sociology of recognition.
paradox-of-tragedy: The paradox of tragedy asks why we take pleasure in watching suffering we would flee in life: tragedy - and horror and the tragic - produces painful emotions that audiences seek out and enjoy. Hume's 'Of Tragedy' set the modern form of the puzzle, and contemporary answers range from conversion theories (pain becomes pleasure by fiction's frame) to appreciation theories (we value the work's power, not the pain itself). The paradox generalizes to 'negative emotions' in all fiction.
value-pluralism: Value pluralism, above all in Isaiah Berlin, is the thesis that genuine human values - liberty and equality, justice and mercy, private happiness and public duty - are objective but multiple, often in conflict, and not commensurable on a single scale. Choices between them are real losses, not clerical bookkeeping, and utopias that promise final harmony are therefore dangerous. The position is a middle road between monism and relativism, and it underwrites Berlin's liberalism.
